A learner's English draft went through a first pass that fixed its small errors. The text as it now reads, sentences numbered:
[S1] I’m on the early chapters of Darktail’s Judgment, and I get a little bit confused about why StarClan didn’t show up when Darkpaw was at the moonstone and he got really miserable and furious because of that.

[S2] Ravenpaw said StarClan had travelled with the Clans and left the forest skies, and it would be hard / not worth it to get back here for a distant little kittypet who wanted to join the Clans.
[S3] But it was mentioned in the book that it was an overcast day, so without the moonlight it makes sense that they couldn’t reach StarClan back then when the Clans were still in the forest.
[S4] (Could someone tell me if there was a similar case in the other books where the night sky was cloudy when a cat was at the Moonstone?
[S5] Or do StarClan have the power to clear the clouds if they want to communicate?)

[S6] And Darkpaw didn’t try again on a clear day; he just chose to turn into Darktail👿 instead.

A tutor found these problems on the draft before the first pass. For each: the words it quoted, the first-pass changes near them (before → after), and the problem as written:
1. quoted: "confused about the plot that StarClan didn't show up"
   changes: "the plot that" → "why"; "went" → "got"; "for" → "because of"
   problem: A reader expects 'plot' to name a storyline element, but here the clause after it is the event itself, so the sentence packs confusion, plot and Darkpaw's reaction into one line. It is hard to see what is confusing.
2. quoted: "(Could someone tell me if there was a similar case"
   changes: "that" → "where"; "sky’s" → "sky was"; "some cat’s" → "a cat was"
   problem: The question sits inside a parenthesis and a nested 'if' clause, so readers must dig to find what is being asked. Ask directly to make the question clear.

The learner now sees only the text as it reads. For each problem: keep false when the first-pass changes already did what the problem asks, so a reader would no longer stumble there; keep true when it is still a problem in the text as it reads. Small corrections (grammar, spelling, a word swapped) only fix problems about those very words: a problem about what the text says or leaves out (a missing point, evidence, a reason), what a reader takes away, or how a sentence is built stays, keep true. For a kept problem: quote, the words of the text as it reads where a reader stumbles now, copied character for character; problem, the same problem said about the text as it reads, in English, at the same length: keep its reasoning and what a reader expects, but never mention an error the first pass fixed (a missing or wrong word, grammar, spelling) and never quote words that are no longer in the text. When nothing in it needs to change, repeat it as it was.
Reply with JSON only: {"spots":[{"id":1,"keep":true,"quote":"","problem":""}]}
